present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD PLACES THIS PERSON NOWHERE ON THE DAY, BECAUSE HE WAS DEAD. A DEATH NOTICE IS NOT A PRESENCE (T-1131): the old settlers' obituary declares `places_in_1835: false` on every record it publishes, because its own header admits it prints citizens who arrived after 1843. persons.note: AN 1833 OR 1834 LIST — POLL, TAX OR MUSTER — WITH ANOTHER SOURCE. Read from death_notice, directory_1843, tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G2b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. death_notice names this person at Chicago by 25 October 1830 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Wolcott, Alexander, City-Hall, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Wolcott, Alexander, | 1834, June 4, | Middletown, Conn. | 64 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. AND THIS CARD CONTRADICTS ITSELF ON THE POINT: it already carries a death notice, “Wolcott, Dr. Alexander”, dated Oct. 25, 1830 — before the register was signed. A man dead by then did not sign it, so either the register's entry is another man of the same name or this card is two men. Nothing is withdrawn and no record is split here; the case is filed in data/research/old_settlers/receptions.json under os_q_registered_after_a_documented_death for the identity master (T-0513). Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 10 times, as “WOLCOTT ALEXANDER”, 1830-09-27 to 1830-09-29: 2 federal land entries — E2NE sec 09 T39N R14E; E2NEVO sec 09 T39N R14E and 8 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 4 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 5 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L5BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL1CHIOT, as printed); lot 8 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L8BL1CHIOT, as printed), 160.00 acres stated in all, for $945.00 (ls0055, ls0056, ls1550, ls1551, ls1552, ls1553, ls1554, ls1555, ls1556, ls1557). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS ILLINOIS, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $685.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. birth_year.note: A BIRTH INTERVAL OUT OF A MAN'S OWN STATEMENT OF HIS AGE. He registered at the Calumet Club's reception to the settlers of Chicago on 27 May 1879 and gave his age as 64: "Wolcott, Alexander, | 1834, June 4, | Middletown, Conn. | 64 | Chicago.". An age of 64 completed years given on that day means the birth falls after 27 May 1814 and on or before 27 May 1815, so the birth year is 1814 or 1815. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth. IT IS A RECOLLECTION, forty-four years after the scene date — better than a recollection about somebody else, and still not a record. birth_year.contradicted_by_the_card: AND THE CARD DOES NOT AGREE WITH IT (T-1179). This card says the person stands on tax_1833, and the interval leaves them 19 in 1833 — under the 20 a poll, tax or muster list is drawn at. That floor is the franchise's line and no source states it, so it is set beside this interval and not used to strike it out. The interval is carried anyway, because the floor it misses is one this project invented and says so — the model carries it under the liberty L-rc-age-conditioning — and a floor nobody can cite may not strike out a reading. Both are printed so that a reader meets the disagreement rather than one side of it.

old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Wolcott, Alex., clerk Steamer Geo. W. Dole, for St. Joseph'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
